title: An Account for Every AI Agent: Credit Card Fees Can't Carry the Machine Economy
dek: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
why: The segment on how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy; agent payments come with hard numbers, while the new-drug section is more opinion than detail.
who: Founders and investors watching AI agent payments, stablecoins and on-chain assets; engineering leads who want to copy how AI restructures the R&D process.
skip: The cold open at 0:00 is a re-cut clip from the main episode and can be skipped.

points.h: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
points.body: Armstrong says agents are already generating a flood of transactions worth a few cents: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialized agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: about 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest argument for stablecoins and crypto rails cutting into the machine economy.

Coinbase has built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has ever had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test that has been run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future cases, and the one-shot PR rate keeps climbing, something Armstrong calls "recursive self-improvement."

points.h: The CEO runs 10 agents changing code at once
points.body: Armstrong says that now, when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day — he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends over a finished PR for review, which he says is addictive. He has also gotten the CEO back to writing features: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten items each, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of doing this podcast, all 10 items got done and were waiting for his review.

points.h: What gets killed is tasks, not people
points.body: On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity really is rising, but that is a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He does not think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people already there can do vastly more and everything speeds up; and yes, two-person and five-person companies will do volumes that were previously unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people produces far more, and over the long run margins should rise. He does not close the door on it — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

points.h: 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
points.body: Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, sees it as digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenized equity product he just announced is currently available only outside the US, and they are talking with regulators about a US path; he stresses that these are real stocks — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

points.h: Prediction markets are more than sports betting
points.body: Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached roughly $100 million in annualized revenue, growing more than 100% quarter over quarter. Sports is indeed part of it, and he sees that as entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it is much bigger than that, and that the societal implications are not yet fully understood. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation." Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God," which he calls an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock — you are just betting on whether it gets better or worse.

points.h: Restore cells to their youthful function
points.body: New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it does not change the cell type (the Yamanaka-lab style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast combinatorial space of transcription factors for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then does functional experiments (mostly in animal models), and finally goes into human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and T cells of the immune system. The first Phase 1 trial is in alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates that this one drug alone, if successful, could be worth $20 billion, but the goal is for a 40-year-old to have the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

points.h: What America lacks is not land, it's a sandbox
points.body: Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places, overregulation. He mentions that Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and he thinks they have had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centers, nuclear power plants, unlimited drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item — first test what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to test in, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.
